findings.title: SQL injection via unvalidated sort column
findings.description: The `sort` parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL string with an f-string instead of being validated against an allowlist of column names. Since `search_expenses` is described as having a 'configurable sort column', an attacker-controlled `sort` value (e.g. `id; DROP TABLE expenses; --` or a UNION-based payload) would be executed verbatim, allowing arbitrary SQL execution against the database.

findings.title: Unescaped LIKE wildcards in search text
findings.description: `text` is inserted into the LIKE pattern without escaping `%` or `_`, so a user's search input containing these characters behaves as unintended SQL wildcards (e.g. `_` matches any single character, and a text of `%` matches every row). This can produce incorrect/overbroad search results and, combined with the note field, may leak more expenses than the note text should match.

findings.title: No result limit or pagination on search results
findings.description: Unlike the other expense-listing query in this file which applies PAGE_SIZE/LIMIT and OFFSET, search_expenses returns every matching row with no LIMIT. A user with many matching expenses (or an adversarial note text like '%') can trigger an unbounded query result, risking excessive memory usage and slow responses.

findings.title: No tests for new search_expenses function
findings.description: The PR adds a new public function with SQL string interpolation and no accompanying tests covering basic search behavior, empty/no-match results, the sort parameter, or malicious inputs (e.g. SQL injection via sort, wildcard characters in text). Given the security-sensitive nature of the interpolated sort clause, this is inadequately tested.
